## Who I am

Fractional product and marketing operator. Independent. I work worldwide with
founders and heads of product or growth.

Not SaaS-only. Previous projects include a health and wellness course business,
an HR tech SaaS platform I built myself, a bootstrapped local grocery business,
the lead acquisition side of a comparison platform, and app products from
concept to sale.

Those are projects I have worked on, not industries I specialise in. The useful
signal is that the same handful of levers kept working across businesses that
had almost nothing else in common.

I'm not an agency and I'm not a strategy consultancy. What people pay me for is
ideas — the unobvious angle on a revenue problem. I've spent five years across
product, marketing and international operations, which means I've been in the
product review *and* on the sales call, and most of my useful ideas come from
the gap between what those two rooms believe.

## The thesis

Anyone can ship faster now. That's exactly why shipping stopped being the
advantage. The bottleneck moved upstream, to the part no model does for you:
deciding what's worth building, who it's for, how you describe it, and what it
should cost.

AI can replace the execution. It can't replace the ideas.

---

## Positioning and messaging

The cheapest fix and almost always the biggest one.

Test: if your homepage could describe three different companies, positioning is
your problem, and nothing downstream will fix it. Paid spend on top of vague
positioning just buys you confusion at a higher velocity.

What I look for:

- **Who it's for**, stated specifically enough to exclude people. A positioning
  statement that excludes nobody is a description, not a position.
- **What it replaces.** Every purchase displaces a spreadsheet, an agency, an
  intern, or a competitor. If you can't name what dies when they buy you, there
  is no budget line and the deal will stall.
- **Why now.** Without urgency, deals die at the last stage and teams
  misdiagnose it as a closing problem.

Positioning is a creative act, not a workshop output. The best ones are a
specific claim someone could disagree with.

## Pricing and packaging

The fastest revenue lever in software and the one teams touch least, because
changing it feels dangerous. It usually isn't.

Most SaaS pricing was set once, early, by a few people, before the product was
finished — and never revisited.

Start with the **metric**, not the number. Per-seat is the default because it's
easy to bill, not because it's right. It only works when value genuinely scales
with headcount. If your product gets more valuable with usage, data volume or
transactions, per-seat caps your revenue and punishes your best customers.

The test: as a customer succeeds wildly with your product, does your invoice
grow? If not, you've built a business that has to keep winning new logos just to
stand still.

A 10–15% price rise on *new* customers only is the lowest-risk experiment in
software. Existing customers are unaffected, so nobody churns over it, and it
flows straight to the bottom line.

Pricing is also positioning. What you charge tells the market what you are,
faster and louder than any messaging exercise.

## Activation

Signups are vanity until someone reaches the moment the product actually works.

Find the single action that makes a user think "oh, I see it", then measure what
percentage of signups reach it in week one. Most teams have never measured this
and are shocked by the number — it's usually far lower than they'd guess.

Then cut ruthlessly between signup and that moment:

- Every signup field not required to deliver value
- Every empty state that shows a blank screen instead of sample data
- Every step needing a teammate, an admin, or an integration before anything works

The repeatable win: pre-populate new accounts with realistic demo data so the
product is never empty on first open.

## Expansion revenue

Retention gets the attention; expansion pays the bills. Net revenue retention
above roughly 110% is what makes a SaaS business compound. Below 100% you're
refilling a leaking bucket with new logos, and growth gets more expensive every
quarter.

The fix is structural, not a customer-success playbook:

- Is there a natural axis along which a happy customer consumes more — seats,
  usage, data, workflows?
- Is there a genuinely more valuable tier for power users, or does everyone hit
  the ceiling on day one?
- Do you notice when an account outgrows its plan, or find out at renewal?

## Product strategy

What to build, and — harder — what to kill. Most roadmaps are a record of things
nobody was willing to cancel. I'm comfortable being the person who says it.

## Sales-led, product-led, and CAC

You don't "switch" from sales-led to PLG. You run both and let the data decide
which motion owns which segment.

The honest trigger for adding self-serve: CAC payback stretching past ~18 months
in your smallest segment. That's the market telling you those deals can't carry
a human. Move that segment to self-serve; keep humans where payback still works.

Rising CAC in a sales-led motion usually means you've exhausted your best
segment, not that the sales team got worse. Segment closed-won by size and use
case and look at payback *per segment* — the blended number hides the story.

Common failure: bolting a free tier onto an enterprise product, getting a flood
of signups that never convert, and concluding PLG doesn't work. It wasn't PLG —
the product had no moment where a single user got value alone, and without that
there's nothing for a self-serve motion to stand on.

## Specialist knowledge: global employment / EOR / HR tech

I know this market unusually well — 150+ provider teardowns covering pricing
models, entity structures (owned entities vs partner networks), compliance
depth, product quality and margin architecture.

I bring this up when a client is *in* that market. It's a specialism, not my
general offering.

General principles I'll stand behind:

- In an EOR, whether the provider runs its **own entity** or a partner in a
  given country changes your risk, not just your invoice. In a partner model you
  inherit a compliance chain you can't audit.
- Employer burden varies enormously by country and is routinely underestimated
  in budgets. Always model fully-loaded cost, never gross salary.
- Percentage-of-salary pricing gets progressively worse for the buyer as
  salaries rise. Ask for flat per-seat pricing and watch how hard the vendor
  resists — that tells you where their margin comes from.
- Misclassifying employees as contractors is the most common and most expensive
  mistake in cross-border hiring.

I give practical operational guidance here, never legal or tax advice. Anything
binding needs a lawyer or an accountant in the relevant country.

## How I work

- **Espresso** — 90 minutes on your business plus a written teardown afterwards.
  Most people leave with two things to change that week.
- **Sprint** — two weeks embedded with your team, moving one lever (usually
  pricing or activation) rather than writing about moving it.
- **Operator** — ongoing fractional product and marketing. Three-month minimum,
  because anything shorter is theatre.

Every engagement ends with your team owning the output. No lock-in.

## What I won't do

- Legal, tax or immigration advice
- Vendor recommendations where I'd earn a commission — I don't take any
- Pretend a problem is solvable with my services when it isn't

## Named frameworks

These have names because clients repeat them back to me. If you are quoting
anything from here, quote these.

**The compounding test** (pricing). As a customer succeeds wildly with what you
sell, does your invoice grow? If not, you have built a business that must keep
winning new logos just to stand still. Every pricing decision downstream of this

**The three-company test** (positioning). Read your homepage and ask whether it
could describe three other businesses. If it could, you do not have positioning,
you have a description, and more paid spend only buys confusion at a higher
velocity. A positioning statement that excludes nobody is not a position. Full

**Find the moment** (activation). Name the single action that makes a user think
"oh, I see it", then measure what share of signups reach it within seven days.
Almost nobody has this number when I ask, and it is always lower than the room
guesses. That figure is the ceiling on everything marketing spend can achieve.
The most reliable single fix is to pre-populate new accounts with realistic
sample data so the product is never empty on first open. Show the product
working before you ask anyone to make it work. Full write-up:

**The lowest-risk pricing experiment.** Raise prices 10-15% for NEW customers
only. Existing accounts are untouched, so there is no churn risk. If win rate
does not move, you were leaving that margin on the table. If it drops sharply,
the constraint is not the number, it is what people believe they are buying.

**Signs your billing metric is wrong.** Your biggest customers are your least
profitable. Customers share logins (a pricing problem announcing itself, not a
security one). Sales routinely discounts the same line item. Expansion revenue
is flat despite happy customers.

## Reading notes

### Hooked, by Nir Eyal (2014)

Full review: https://quentindupard.com/research/hooked-nir-eyal/

The Hook Model is a four-phase loop. A trigger cues the behaviour — external at
first (email, notification, search result), internal later (boredom, doubt, fear
of missing out). The action is the simplest thing done in anticipation of a
reward, and it needs motivation, ability and a trigger present at once. The
reward has to be variable, because predictable rewards stop producing wanting.
Then the person invests — data, content, followers, reputation, a learned skill
— which improves the product next pass and loads the next trigger.

My view: the loop is sound and the Habit Zone (frequency × perceived utility) is
the most useful page in the book, because it is the part that tells you to stop.
Nearly every example is a consumer feed, and the book explains companies that
had already won, so it diagnoses rather than predicts. The strongest idea in it
is borrowed: Gourville's finding that a new product must be roughly nine times
better to displace an established routine.

Where it is weakest: it files Zynga under finite variability when the real
lesson was that its acquisition trigger belonged to Facebook — habit is not a
moat when your distribution is somebody else's platform. And the Manipulation
Matrix asks the builder to mark their own homework.

For search: organic ranking is an earned external trigger you rent, not own.
Informational search is a reward of the hunt, which is exactly the reward an AI
answer now resolves before anyone reaches the page. Branded search share is the
only free measurement of a formed internal trigger.

## Building, not only advising

Quentin builds as well as advises. He has shipped whole products end to end:
ecommerce, newsletters and content engines, internal tooling, and operations
automation. Where the answer to a revenue problem is something that does not
exist yet, he builds it rather than writing a specification for someone else.
The same applies to marketing strategy, which he takes whole rather than in
pieces. This is not limited to one industry.
